body.text: The Taliban regime in Afghanistan is facing a new internal threat – the Afghanistan United Front (AUF), also known as the Afghan United Front. Led by Sami Sadat, a former commander of the Afghan Army’s Special Forces, the AUF was launched in 2023 in the United States with the aim to “liberate Afghanistan from the occupation of the Taliban, drive out extremist groups and work for the welfare of Afghan citizens.”

On its official website, the group mentions that the “freedom of Afghanistan” is its vision and that its mission is “to unite Afghans and return Afghanistan to the constitutional order, ensuring that Afghans can enjoy freedom, peace, and prosperity.” Even though the group was founded as a political movement, as its vision and mission statements clearly manifest, it has increased physical attacks against the de facto government in Afghanistan since the beginning of August 2026.

In August, the AUF announced the launch of a military campaign, “Operation Muharib,” against the Taliban. At the onset of the operation, Sadat said that he authorized “members of Afghanistan United Front to begin combat operations against the Taliban.” He added that the phase of operations would include the “Taliban members, bases and their leadership.” He stressed that “our war is for freedom. Afghans are freedom-loving people,” and talked about the Taliban’s atrocities during the last five years, announcing that it was time “we take our fate in our own hands and embark on the armed struggle to free our people from the Taliban tyranny.”

While addressing the neighboring countries, Sadat said that “we have a very clear vision. We want to free Afghanistan from the Taliban regime.” He claimed that the Taliban were involved in supporting terror groups in their “malicious intents against the neighboring states and the rest of the world.”

Within the first month of its announced operation, the AUF claimed that it had carried out approximately 43 attacks targeting the Taliban in 14 provinces. During these attacks, 74 Taliban members were killed, and 35 were wounded, the group asserted. The group further claimed that the attacks were targeted at individuals allegedly involved in harassing, torturing, and arresting citizens of Afghanistan. Hilal Kakar, a spokesman for the group, said that one of these attacks was executed against the Taliban army corps in Kandahar and another was a targeted attack on the regime’s military base in Helmand province’s Nawzad district.

The following month, in September, the AUF claimed to have conducted 21 attacks across Afghanistan, killing 21 Taliban members and injured at least nine more. In these attacks, the group seemed determined to target the Taliban’s strongholds, as six attacks were carried out in Kandahar and three in Helmand, both in southern Afghanistan, where the Taliban’s base of power is centered. Most of the group’s attacks consisted of either ambushes or assassinations targeting individual members of the Taliban. Some of the attacks were directed at outposts and checkpoints. The AUF also claimed that its members attacked the Taliban’s governor’s office in Ghor province in central Afghanistan on September 28. The Taliban forces detained at least 10 people for their alleged connection to the attack in Firozkoh, the capital of Ghor province.

In October, the AUF claimed 36 attacks, with most attacks in Helmand and Kandahar as in previous months. On October 26, the group claimed on its news website, “Road to Freedom,” that its forces executed seven attacks in six of Afghanistan’s provinces, including Badakhshan, Ghazni, Ghor, Kandahar, Parwan, and Zabul. During these attacks, all within 24 hours, nine Taliban members were killed, and more than nine were injured. After the attacks, the AUF posted on its official X account, “Our operations will continue until the complete liberation of Afghanistan from the tyranny of the Taliban and the return of the will of the nation.”

The AUF’s leader, Sadat, describes its attacks as combat operations. The group has claimed to have conducted a total of 126 attacks across 22 of the 34 provinces of Afghanistan between August 1 and November 13, 2026. In these attacks, it claims to have killed 135 and injured 60 members of the Taliban regime. Out of the 126 attacks claimed, 37 were carried out in Kandahar and 27 in Helmand. Along with these attacks targeting Taliban members, the group also runs a military court department, which so far has ordered the execution of six individuals “convicted of spying for the Taliban and other offenses,” as per the claims of its spokesman Hilal Kakar.

The emergence of the AUF as an anti-Taliban military group has given rise to more attacks against the Taliban; other groups have also been increasing their operations in recent months. Among those groups, the most prominent are Ahmad Massoud’s National Resistance Front (NRF); the Afghan Freedom Front (AFF), founded by Former Afghan National Army Chief of General Staff Yasin Zia; Green Unit, the military wing of the Green Trend which was founded by Former First Vice President and National Directorate of Security director Amrullah Saleh; the Afghan Liberation Movement (ALM); the Freedom and Justice Movement; the National Mobilization Front; and a newly formed armed group dubbed Sepahiyan-e Mihan (Patriotic Soldiers Front).

Although many of these groups have claimed an increase in their activities, the AUF’s way of conducting attacks is different. Unlike other groups, the AUF targets the stronghold of the Taliban in the southern provinces, mainly Kandahar and Helmand. It not limited itself to one province and has expanded its operations across at least 22 provinces. Additionally, it records and publicizes its attacks against Taliban members in a way other groups have not.

The AUF has made quite a statement in a short period of time, something many other groups have not been able to do over the last five years. The group’s targeted and precise attacks and ambushes against Taliban members make it stand out from other anti-Taliban groups. In his inaugural statement in August, Sadat asked Afghans inside the country and those abroad to join the fight for freedom, but the question remains whether Afghans will be ready to join together to defeat the Taliban.
